iterations.narrative:
The RaMP enrichment analysis reveals a dominant signal centred on **galactose metabolism and galactosemia**, with five metabolites — galactitol, myo-inositol, sucrose, galactinol, and glycerol — achieving near-perfect enrichment (fold > 870, FDR ≈ 0) in both the KEGG Galactose Metabolism pathway (map00052) and the SMPDB Galactosemia module (SMP00182). A secondary glycerophospholipid axis is also implicated (FDR = 10⁻⁶), with glycerol, myo-inositol, choline, and O-phosphoethanolamine driving that signal.

Within the galactose metabolism network, **galactitol (C01697)** is the hallmark driver: it is the terminal polyol that accumulates when galactose cannot be further metabolised, and it is confirmed as a direct member of the pathway. **Galactinol (C01235)** and **myo-inositol (C00137)** are likewise confirmed members, connected in the reaction graph via a one-hop bidirectional edge (myo-inositol ↔ galactinol). Tracing upstream, sucrose (C00089) feeds into the pathway through glucose and galactose en route to myo-inositol and galactinol (path length 5, forward direction), identifying sucrose as a plausible upstream trigger of the observed accumulation pattern.

The biological picture is consistent with a **galactose overload or enzymatic impairment** of the Leloir pathway. Elevated galactitol reflects reduced aldehyde detoxification capacity, a hallmark of classic galactosemia. The co-enrichment of glycerophospholipid metabolites (choline, O-phosphoethanolamine) hints at broader membrane-homeostasis stress, which is recognised in galactosemia models where galactolipid accumulation perturbs neural and hepatic membranes. The presence of butanone and guanabenz is less pathognomonic but may reflect secondary carbonyl stress and adrenergic-response modulation reported in metabolic liver disease. The convergence of five high-confidence pathway members on this hub makes galactose metabolism the primary affected system.

The biological picture is consistent with **galactose metabolism dysfunction** reflected in the Galactose Metabolism (KEGG map00052) and Galactosemia (SMP00182) pathways. **Limitations:** The choline and O-phosphoethanolamine signals could not be verified as drivers of the galactose metabolism pathway, and their inclusion as secondary-axis drivers rests on weaker or absent pathway-membership evidence. Additional targeted follow-up is needed to characterise their contribution.
